instruction: Why do I have to wear this bracelet on my arm?
response: That bracelet is really important! It has your name and birthday on it, and a special barcode. Before the doctors or nurses give you any medicine or do a test, they check your bracelet to make sure everything is exactly right for you. Think of it like a super-special name tag that helps keep you safe the whole time you're here.

instruction: Can my mom bring my dog to visit me?
response: I know you must really miss your dog! Pets from home aren't usually allowed to visit because we need to keep all the kids here safe and healthy. But guess what — sometimes specially trained therapy dogs come to visit kids in the hospital! You could ask your nurse if there's a therapy dog visit coming up on your unit. That might be a fun surprise!

instruction: I'm hungry. When is dinner?
response: Dinner trays usually come between 4:45 and 5:45 in the evening. Before you eat anything, though, your nurse needs to say it's okay — sometimes there are special reasons a kid might need to wait. If your tummy is really rumbling and it's not dinnertime yet, ask your parent or guardian to check with your nurse about getting a snack from the pantry.

instruction: Why does everyone keep squirting that stuff on their hands?
response: Great question! That's hand sanitizer, and it kills tiny germs you can't even see. Everybody — nurses, doctors, your family, and visitors — cleans their hands when they come into your room and when they leave. It's one of the best ways to stop germs from spreading so kids like you can get better faster. You can use it too!

instruction: Can I go play in the hallway?
response: The hallways are really busy with carts and people moving around, so it's safest to stay in your room or go to one of the special play spaces. There's a cool activity room on the sixth floor called the School-Age Activity Room where you can do crafts, play board games, build with LEGO, and lots more. Ask your nurse or your parent if you can go check it out!

instruction: Why can't I sleep in the same bed as my mommy?
response: I know it would feel really cozy to snuggle up together, but the nurses need to be able to reach you quickly whenever they come to check on you, even in the middle of the night. Your mom can sleep right beside you, though — there's a special sleep space for a parent right next to your bed. So she'll be super close all night long.

instruction: Can I bring all my stuffed animals?
response: You can definitely bring a few favourite stuffed animals to help your room feel more like home! The hospital does ask that you don't bring too many, though, because the nurses need space around your bed to take care of you and keep things clean. Pick your top favourites — ones that can be wiped down or washed are the best choice. And remember, your stuffies should stay with you and not be shared with other kids, just to keep everyone healthy.

instruction: There's a scary machine that beeps when I walk through the door downstairs. What is it?
response: That machine is there to help keep everyone in the hospital safe. It checks to make sure nobody is bringing anything inside that could be dangerous. You just walk right through it — you don't have to stop or take anything off. If it makes a little sound, a friendly security guard might take a quick look, but it's nothing to worry about at all. It's kind of like the ones at the airport!

instruction: Why do the nurses keep waking me up at night?
response: I know it can be annoying to get woken up when you're cozy and sleepy! The nurses check on you during the night to make sure you're doing okay — things like making sure you're comfortable and safe. It's actually a really caring thing they do for every kid here. Try to close your eyes again right after and you'll drift back to sleep. You're doing great!

instruction: My friend wants to come visit. Can she come whenever she wants?
response: It's awesome that your friend wants to visit! Visiting times can be a little different depending on which part of the hospital you're in, so the best thing to do is have your parent ask your nurse about the best times for visitors. Also, it's really important that your friend only comes if she's feeling totally healthy — no coughs, sniffles, or tummy bugs. That way everyone stays safe!

instruction: What are the visiting hours here? My friends want to come see me but I don't want them showing up at a bad time.
response: Visiting hours can vary depending on which unit you're on, so there isn't one set schedule for the whole hospital. Your best bet is to ask the nurses on your unit about the times that work best. A couple of things worth passing along to your friends: visitors should avoid nursing shift changes, which happen from about 6:45 to 7:30 in the morning and evening. And anyone who's been feeling sick in the past week should hold off on visiting — it's a safety thing for all the patients on the floor.

instruction: I really need some fresh air. Can I step outside to vape?
response: I totally get wanting fresh air — being stuck inside is rough. But the entire hospital property, including the grounds and parking lots, is completely smoke-free under Ontario law. That covers cigarettes, vapes, e-cigarettes, and anything else you can smoke or inhale. If you're feeling restless or stressed, you could let your care team know — there are people here like Child Life Specialists who can help you find ways to cope while you're admitted.

instruction: My unit door is locked and I need a code to get in and out. Why is that?
response: If you're on the B6 inpatient unit, it's a locked unit for everyone's safety and security. When you were admitted, your family should have gotten a confidential access code. The locked doors help the staff keep track of who's coming and going so that all the patients on the floor stay safe. If you need to leave and come back — like heading to the activity room or the family lounge — just use that code, and let your nurse know you're stepping out.

instruction: Do I actually have to wear this hospital ID band the whole time? It's kind of annoying.
response: Yeah, I hear you — it's not exactly a fashion statement. But that ID band is a key part of how the hospital keeps you safe. It has your name, date of birth, hospital ID number, and a barcode on it. Staff scan or check it before giving you any medication, running tests, or taking you anywhere for a procedure. If you have allergies, you'll also have a red allergy bracelet so every person on your care team is aware. It needs to stay on for your entire stay.

instruction: Can my parents actually stay overnight with me or do they have to leave?
response: In most patient rooms at Children's Hospital, there's a sleep space set up for a parent or caregiver to stay overnight right by your bed. Clean sheets, pillows, and blankets are provided. If you're in the PCCU, there are two sleep spaces at the bedside plus a quiet room and a sleep room nearby. Family members who are staying between 8 p.m. and 8 a.m. are just asked to stay in your room and let the unit staff know when they arrive or leave.

instruction: Is there Wi-Fi here? I need to get on my phone.
response: Yes — patients are encouraged to use their own phones to stay connected with friends and family. There's a patient entertainment site where you can access your own streaming accounts too. If you run into any trouble connecting to the Wi-Fi, you or your family can call the Data Valet line at 1-800-642-3958 for help getting set up.

instruction: What's the deal with the fragrance-free policy? My aunt wants to bring me some stuff.
response: The whole hospital is fragrance-free. That means no perfume, cologne, scented lotions, body sprays, or anything with a strong scent. The reason is that some patients and staff have serious allergies or respiratory conditions, and fragrances can trigger reactions. So if your aunt is bringing you care items, go for the unscented versions of things like deodorant, lotion, or shampoo. It's one of those rules that's easy to follow once you know about it.

instruction: Someone on my care team mentioned a bedside shift change report. What is that and do I have to be involved?
response: It's basically the handoff that happens when one nurse's shift ends and the next one starts. They'll come to your bedside together, and the outgoing nurse fills the incoming nurse in on your care plan and how things have been going. It takes about three to five minutes. You and your family are invited to listen in, ask questions, and share anything you think is important — but it's not forced. You get to participate in whatever way feels comfortable for you.

instruction: I want to order food from outside the hospital. Are there any rules about that?
response: There's no blanket ban on outside food, but there's a really important step first: always check with your care team before eating or drinking anything. Depending on your situation, you might be on a specific prescribed diet or there may be medical reasons you need to avoid certain foods. If your team gives the okay, just make sure to label and date anything you store in the family fridge so it doesn't get tossed. The Tim Hortons on the second floor of Zone B is also an option on weekdays between 6:30 a.m. and 8 p.m.

instruction: After 8:30 p.m. the main entrance was locked and I had to talk to a security guard to get in. Is that normal?
response: Totally normal. The B Tower main entrance is open from 6:00 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. every day. After that, access is controlled by Security — you just need to check in with the guard and they'll let you through. If you come in through the parking garage entrance, that's open 24 hours, but you'll still need to check in with Security after hours. It's all about keeping patients safe, especially overnight. If you ever need a security escort to your car or to the Ronald McDonald House, you can call extension 52281.
